paras: The whipping of Bibb County chain gang convicts was the beating of two Black convicts by a guard of the county chain gang in Bibb County, Georgia, reported in November 1882. The Bibb County grand jury proposed to investigate the case, and within days the county's Road Commissioners gave up control of the chain gang to the County Commissioners.

According to the Savannah Morning News, two "negro convicts" then serving on the Bibb County chain gang had been "cruelly whipped and beaten by those having them in charge." A follow-up item in the same paper named the man who whipped them as Charles Thomas, one of the guards. Neither report gave the convicts' names, the date or place of the whipping, the reason for it, or the extent of their injuries.

By 21 November 1882 the Bibb County grand jury had announced that it proposed to investigate the case. The whipping "considerably unsettled things" for the Road Commissioners, who had worked and controlled the gang for several years, and on Saturday, 25 November, they turned control of it over to the County Commissioners. The County Commissioners took direction of the gang and elected James Amison its superintendent.
No report of the grand jury's findings, or of any indictment, trial or dismissal of the guard, appears in the coverage.

The case surfaced only as two short paragraphs in the Savannah Morning News's "Georgia and Florida" state-news column, on 21 and 29 November 1882, set among fires, railroad accidents and crop reports. The first item described the whipping as cruel and framed it as a matter for the grand jury, while the second treated it chiefly as an administrative question of who should control the convict gang. Both identified the victims only by race and status as "negro convicts."
